claims.text: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys, the balance between mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch controls phase stability.
Near-equiatomic compositions maximize free-energy stabilization of a solid-solution phase.
The free-energy-stabilized phase at equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition is single-phase FCC.
A single FCC phase in equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni retains an optimal combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Small systematic deviations from equiatomic composition, especially changes in Al and Ni, promote secondary-phase nucleation.
Secondary-phase formation caused by Al or Ni deviations degrades high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The initial equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy exhibits a single-phase FCC structure.
Al and Ni concentrations will be varied systematically away from an equiatomic baseline using combinatorial synthesis.
The controlled comparison will include high-temperature thermal cycling, irradiation exposure, and cryogenic mechanical testing.
Compositional changes alter mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch.
Changes in mixing enthalpy and atomic-size mismatch change the Gibbs free-energy difference between single-phase FCC and multiphase states.
Disruption of the proposed thermodynamic balance causes secondary phases to nucleate within the FCC matrix.
The equiatomic alloy will remain single-phase FCC during the specified thermal, irradiation, and cryogenic tests.
Increasing or decreasing Al and/or Ni will produce XRD- or microscopy-detectable secondary phases earlier than in the equiatomic baseline.
The appearance of secondary phases will correlate with degradation of mechanical and environmental properties.
Processing history and grain structure may modulate the proposed composition–phase–property trends.
The hypothesis is limited to controlled processing and a narrow range of compositional deviations.
A lack of both phase-stability differences and correlated property degradation relative to the equiatomic baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
